Learning Objectives

Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:

  • 01Explain the purpose of dissolve, proximity, buffering, and overlay operations, and describe the kinds of spatial questions each one can answer.
  • 02Use ArcGIS Pro to perform common geoprocessing operations — Dissolve, Buffer, Clip, Intersect, Union, and Erase — and interpret the outputs they produce.
  • 03Distinguish between Euclidean and geodesic buffers and explain when geodesic distance is more appropriate across large areas.
  • 04Compare vector overlay and raster overlay and identify how geometry, attributes, and cell values are combined in each approach.

Dissolve

A dissolve is primarily used to combine similar features within a data layer based on their attributes. Boundaries between neighboring features are removed wherever those features share the same value for a chosen “dissolve” attribute, merging them into a single, larger feature.

A dissolve can produce dramatic space savings and complexity reduction. In the example below the number of polygons is reduced roughly nine-fold — from 1,074 on the left to 119 on the right.

We often want to transfer or summarize information in the attribute table while dissolving. For example, we might report the average forest stand age for each forest type.

Proximity functions & distance

Proximity operations are among the most powerful and common spatial-analysis tools. Many important questions hinge on proximity — the distance between features of interest:

  • QHow close are schools to an oil refinery?
  • QWhich neighborhoods are far from convenience stores?
  • QWhich homes will be affected by an increase in freeway noise?

Proximity functions modify existing features or create new ones that depend in some way on distance. One simple proximity function is distance accumulation: it creates a raster of the minimum distance from a set of features. Every output cell stores how far it is from the nearest target feature, so distance “spreads outward” across the whole surface.

Distance values are most often calculated with the Pythagorean formula, typically measured from the closest target cell center to every other cell center.

Buffering

Buffering is one of the most commonly used proximity functions. A buffer is a region that is less than or equal to a specified distance from one or more features.

  • •Buffers can be built for point, line, or area features, and for raster or vector data.
  • •They identify areas that are inside vs. outside a given threshold distance.

Example buffer questions:

  • •Emergency planners may wish to know which schools are within 1.5 kilometers of an earthquake fault
  • •A park planner may wish to identify all lands more than 10 kilometers from the nearest highway, or a business owner may wish to identify all potential customers within a given radius of her store
  • •A natural resources manager may wish to identify major roads that are 10 meters from deer activity

Raster buffering is a two-step process

With raster data, a buffer is built by following these two steps:

  • 1Calculate distance from the features.
  • 2Reclassify cells: those closer than the threshold become “inside” the buffer; those farther become “outside.”

Because raster distance is measured between cell centers, a raster buffer often has a “stair-step” boundary rather than a smooth edge.

Vector buffers

Vector buffering can be applied to point, line, or area features, but regardless of the input, it always produces area (polygon) output. The output polygon is the set of all locations within the buffer distance of the input — so even a single point becomes a circle, and a line becomes a corridor.

Simple buffering applies one uniform distance to every feature — e.g. a 100 m buffer on every road, regardless of road size or type.

Several variants extend this idea:

  • •Compound buffers keep all overlapping boundaries instead of dissolving them into one area.
  • •Nested (multiring) buffers build buffers at several distances around the same feature.
  • •Variable-distance buffers let the buffer distance change from one feature to another.

Euclidean vs. geodesic buffers

Euclidean buffers measure distance in a flat, projected coordinate system, while geodesic buffers measure distance along the curved surface of the Earth — which better represents true real-world distance over large areas.

The figure below uses the Mercator projection, which distorts area and distance, especially near the poles. Near the equator, where distortion is lowest, the Euclidean and geodesic buffers look similar; farther from the equator they diverge as distortion increases.

Introducing overlay

Overlays combine spatial and attribute data from two or more layers, and they are among the most common and powerful spatial operations.

Example overlay questions:

  • •Where can I find inexpensive houses in good school districts?
  • •Where do whale feeding grounds overlap with proposed oil drilling areas?
  • •Which farm fields are on highly erodible soils?
  • •Where do deer home ranges overlap with residential land use?

Vector overlay

Overlay in the vector data model combines the point, line, and polygon geometry and the associated attribute data from two layers into a new layer — creating new geometry in the process.

Clip

A clip is a “cookie-cutter” overlay. A bounding polygon layer defines the clipping region, and only the input features inside it are kept.

Intersect

An intersection fuses data from both layers, but only for the area where both layers contain data.

Union

A union retains all data from both layers — overlapping and non-overlapping areas alike.

Erase

The erase function removes part of an input layer using another feature as the erase feature. It is especially useful when updating a layer — old or lower-quality data can be erased and newer data substituted.

Quick intuition for the four tools: Clip and Erase use one layer as a stencil (keep inside / remove inside) and carry only the first layer’s attributes; Intersect and Union merge attributes from both layers, keeping either just the overlap (Intersect) or everything (Union).

A common problem: slivers

Vector overlay can create slivers — small gaps or spurious polygons along a boundary that two layers represent slightly differently. Slivers can be detected and removed manually or automatically. They usually appear because the “same” boundary was digitized from two different sources, so the two versions don’t line up exactly.

Raster overlay

Raster overlay involves the cell-by-cell combination of two or more layers. A cell in one layer corresponds to the cell in the same location in another layer; their values are combined in some way, and the result is written to the matching cell in an output layer.

For a raster overlay to be unambiguous, the input layers should line up — matching cell size, extent, and alignment — so that each output cell draws from exactly one cell in every input.

An example workflow using overlay

In practice, spatial operations are often sequential, forming a workflow: the output of one operation becomes the input to the next.

Our goal: identify suitable areas for wind farms, based on two criteria —

  • 1High average wind speed — energy output increases with wind speed.
  • 2Low population density — land is cheaper and there are fewer neighbors to disturb.

Wind speed

Reclassify the continuous wind-speed surface into a simple wind class (e.g. high vs. low) using a threshold.

Population

Do the same for population: reclassify density into sparse vs. dense.

Overlay

Finally, overlay the wind-class and population-class layers and select cells that are high wind and low population — the suitable sites.

Try it — sketch the workflow

Suppose you also need sites to be within 5 km of an existing transmission line — the high-voltage power lines that carry electricity long distances from power plants toward the towns and substations that use it. In one or two sentences, describe where that criterion fits into the workflow above and which operation you’d use for it. Post your answer to the course discussion board.

Key takeaways

1
Dissolve merges adjacent features that share an attribute value, simplifying a dataset while allowing attribute summaries such as sums or averages.
2
Proximity operations answer distance questions; buffers build zones around features to separate what is inside from what is outside a threshold distance.
3
Euclidean buffers use flat, projected distance; geodesic buffers follow the Earth’s curve — the difference grows as projection distortion increases.
4
Overlay combines geometry and attributes from multiple layers. Clip, Intersect, Union, and Erase differ in whether they keep only the overlap, all areas, or remove selected areas; raster overlay instead combines layers cell by cell.
5
Operations are often chained into a workflow, where each output becomes the next input.
